pr_body:
Closes #9031 

**Syntax for end users remains unchanged.**

Changes:
* Renamed `WhenThen` to `Then`
* Split `WhenThenThen` into `ChainedWhen` and `ChainedThen`.
  * This allows us to enforce a valid when-then chain and have nice auto-completion!
  * Technically, we could have only `ChainedWhen` and `ChainedThen` - we don't need `When`/`Then`. But I figured I would keep them to avoid allocating a vector for the most common case which is single when/then without a chain.
* Make `Then` and `ChainedThen` inherit from `Expr`.
  * This replaces the `getattr` hack
  * You now get nice auto-completion on these objects.
  * These objects now pass `isinstance` checks for `Expr`, which is great and will solve a lot of hidden bugs.
pr_comments: @ritchie46 Mind taking a look at this one?
@ritchie46 Could you take a moment to check the Rust side here? I think it's a nice usability improvement, but I'd like to be sure that I'm not introducing any performance penalties here.

issue_context.title: Formalize relationship between `Expr` and `WhenThen`/`WhenThenThen`
issue_context.body:
### Problem description

A lot of our functions/methods look something like this:

```python
def do_stuff(input: int | Expr) -> Expr:
    if isinstance(input, Expr):
        ...
    else:
        ...
```

This looks fine, but it does not handle when/then inputs properly. If I input `pl.when(True).then(1)`, I want it to be treated as an expression.

We can fix the type hint pretty easily - there is already a type alias for it (`PolarsExprType`). But the `isinstance` check is a bit more tricky. I considered:
* making `WhenThen` inherit from `Expr` -> I think this will result in unexpected behaviour
* creating an abstract superclass that both inherit from -> Could work, but what should it be named?
* using a metaclass for both

I'm looking for input on how to handle this elegantly. Maybe @alexander-beedie has an idea?
comments:
Basically you are running into the problem that currently the whole `When/WhenThen/WhenThenThen` is a special construct, but in some ways are like normal expressions.
 
I can't find my comment on an issue on `WhenThen` anymore, but I have proposed before a syntax to allow
```python
expr.whenthen(<if True>, <value if True>, <value if False, default to expr>)
```
which you could chain and use like normal expressions. This can currently be replicated by doing:

```python
pl.when(<if True>).then(<value if true>).otherwise(expr).alias(expr.meta.output_name())
```
which returns a normal expression. If we were to only have that, and remove the complexity of `WhenThen` from the api, your problem would not exist.

So to me it seems we should give it a thought whether we like the current `WhenThen` enough to keep it around, or use a `whenthen()` method on the `Expression` class per the above.

Some cons I can think off (apart from removing existing valid syntax):
1. the syntax is slightly less intuitive, `pl.when().then().otherwise()` reads like `if-else`
2. the order of evaluation on chained `WhenThens` switches around (rightmost takes precedence), which may be confusing, or not? Although I dont think you should chain much, most often that indicates you should be using other methods such as `map_dict`.
3. Possibly less efficient, as there is always the `Otherwise`? But that is a requirement to make it a proper expression on the way out.

Pro's of the new syntax:
1. if you want to override a field based on a condition, `.whenthen()`, due to original field being the default, is more intuitive vs `pl.when().then().otherwise()` which has `null` as the placeholder value.

I realise it is probably not so simple, and I'm sure someone will chime in here to stop me from removing API surface... 

EDIT: 

thinking about this more, and going back to the original issue, `WhenThen`, given it is a "not finished expression", has very few things in common with normal expressions. Instead it wraps around expressions, and leaves you at the `else/otherwise` state until you explicitly close it with `otherwise`. So your original ask:

> pl.when(True).then(1), I want it to be treated as an expression.

Cannot be treated as a normal expression currently, as that would mean you have an implicit `otherwise` applied to it. I don't see how this can be made to work transparently. The only solution would be to have a single `whenthen` method that closes the if-else, i.e. `pl.when(True).then(1, <if False>)`, in which case I would argue my syntax of `pl.lit(1).whenthen(True, <default to 1 here>)` is nicer.

Thanks for the great input, @zundertj. I'm going to let this sink in a bit.

> 3. Possibly less efficient, as there is always the Otherwise? But that is a requirement to make it a proper expression on the way out.

This is a non-issue - we already have code in place that adds the `otherwise` clause automatically, see:
* https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/e03183f55189b92a63128868f398f3d66dd93e80/py-polars/polars/functions/whenthen.py#L145-L147
* https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/e03183f55189b92a63128868f398f3d66dd93e80/py-polars/polars/utils/_parse_expr_input.py#L70-L71
I really don't want to change the syntax. I really like the `if {branch} else {branch}` analogy ( a lot).
I don't think this functionality has to fall under the `WhenThen` umbrella at all. I think a function like `expr2.replace_with_if(value_expr, predicate_expr)` would be easier to read.

I agree it makes sense to treat the result of a `.then()` as an expression that additionally has support for the `when` and `otherwise` methods. Obviously much easier said than done.

@stinodego - When you mention unexpected behaviour caused by inheriting from Expr, for my own understanding, what would that be? Or what would be an example of it?

I think there's also an additional consideration in that after chaining, both `when()` and `then()` return an instance of `WhenThenThen`

E.g. 
```python
(
    type(pl.when(True).then(True).when(True)) == 
    type(pl.when(True).then(True).when(True).then(True))
)
```

If you want treat the result of a `.then()` as an expression, then by extension, an instance of `WhenThenThen` would need to be that. But, at the same time, I don't think you'd ever want the result of `when()` (i.e. also sometimes instance of `WhenThenThen`) to behave as an expression...
You could alternatively "allow" it to have expression methods and just throw an error at run time.

This is kind of the same as what happens when you do `pl.when().then().when().otherwise()`. 
`otherwise` is a hinted method at this stage but it panics at run time. The error message is pretty clear/unambigious though.

One further question - what is the purpose of the `WhenThenThen` class?
Would it be possible instead to create an instance of `When` (instead of `WhenThenThen`) when calling `WhenThen.then()`?

In theory, if you were able to just oscillate between `When` and `WhenThen`, you would also not provide completion/highlighting for the invalid `pl.when().then().when().otherwise()`

Any thoughts or answers much appreciated

I just looked at this, and it can be fixed by making WhenThen / WhenThenThen inherit from Expr. I have a PR in the works.

Also not sure exactly why we need WhenThenThen at all - would be nice if we could get rid of it.

review_comments: Because `WhenThenThen` is split into two structs that 'alternate', it's now impossible to end up with an invalid chain. You can only call `when` after a `then` call and vice versa, and you can only call `otherwise` after a `then` call. So this check is no longer needed.
